# Mechanism of Ca2+ transport by ferroportin ## Authors - Jiemin Shen1 ([ORCID: 0000-0002-3977-0681](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3977-0681)) - Azaan Saalim Wilbon1 - Ming Zhou1 † - Yaping Pan1 ([ORCID: 0000-0001-7459-4217](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-7459-4217)) † ### Affiliations 1. Verna and Marrs McLean Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Baylor College of Medicine Houston United States ([ROR:02pttbw34](https://ror.org/02pttbw34)) † Corresponding author ## Abstract Ferroportin (Fpn) is a transporter that releases ferrous ion (Fe2+) from cells and is important for homeostasis of iron in circulation. Export of one Fe2+ by Fpn is coupled to import of two H+ to maintain charge balance. Here, we show that human Fpn (HsFpn) binds to and mediates Ca2+ transport. We determine the structure of Ca2+-bound HsFpn and identify a single Ca2+ binding site distinct from the Fe2+ binding sites. Further studies validate the Ca2+ binding site and show that Ca2+ transport is not coupled to transport of another ion. In addition, Ca2+ transport is significantly inhibited in the presence of Fe2+ but not vice versa. Function of Fpn as a Ca2+ uniporter may allow regulation of iron homeostasis by Ca2+. ## Introduction Ferroportin (Fpn), encoded by the SLC40A1 gene, is the only known Fe2+ exporter in human (Nemeth and Ganz, 2021; Abboud and Haile, 2000; Donovan et al., 2000; McKie et al., 2000). Fpn is highly expressed on enterocytes, hepatocytes, and macrophages, and mediates release of iron stored in cells (Drakesmith et al., 2015; Mackenzie and Garrick, 2005; Knutson et al., 2005). Activity of Fpn is regulated by hepcidin, a small peptide hormone secreted by hepatocytes, which binds to Fpn and reduces iron export by inhibiting its transport activity and triggering endocytosis of Fpn (Aschemeyer et al., 2018; Nemeth et al., 2004; Nemeth and Ganz, 2021). Mutations in Fpn cause hereditary hemochromatosis and iron-loading anemias in human (Pietrangelo, 2017; Ganz, 2013; Ginzburg, 2019; Vlasveld et al., 2019). We have shown previously that Fpn is a Fe2+/2H+ exchanger, that is, the export of one Fe2+ is accompanied by the import of two H+ (Pan et al., 2020). The electroneutral transport mechanism is likely an adaptation to overcome the negative resting membrane potential that would have significantly hindered export of cations. Structures of mammalian Fpn show two transition-metal ion binding sites, termed Site 1 (S1) and Site 2 (S2) (Billesbølle et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2020). Curiously, each ion binding site is composed of only two residues, Asp39 and His43 for S1, and Cys326 and His507 for S2, and it remains unsettled how S1 and S2 mediate coupled transport of Fe2+ and H+. In the current study, we found that Asp39 is also part of a Ca2+ binding site, and that mutation Asp39Ala almost completely eliminates Ca2+ transport but has a modest impact on Fe2+ transport, suggesting that S1 and S2 may have different roles in Fe2+ or H+ transport. Ca2+ is known to bind to mammalian Fpn (Deshpande et al., 2018), but Ca2+ transport by Fpn has not been demonstrated and the role of Ca2+ in Fe2+ transport remains ambiguous. Using Fpn expressed in Xenopus oocytes, Deshpande et al. found that Fe2+ export requires Ca2+, but Ca2+ is not transported by Fpn (Deshpande et al., 2018). More recently, several studies using purified Fpn reconstituted into liposomes found that Fe2+ transport occurs in the absence of Ca2+ (Li et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2020; Billesbølle et al., 2020), and that Ca2+ could potentiate Fe2+ transport under certain conditions (Li et al., 2020; Billesbølle et al., 2020). In the current study, we visualize the Ca2+ binding site in HsFpn and we demonstrate that Ca2+ is transported by Fpn. We then examine the mechanism of Ca2+ transport and its effect on Fe2+ transport. ## Results ### HsFpn is a Ca2+ uniporter HsFpn was expressed, purified, and reconstituted into liposomes for transport assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and Materials and methods). Significant Ca2+ uptake was observed in proteoliposomes reconstituted with HsFpn, as indicated by increased fluorescence of Fluo-4 trapped inside of the vesicles (Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b). In contrast, control liposomes that do not have HsFpn show minimal change in fluorescence (Figure 1a). We also found that Ca2+ transport is inhibited by hepcidin and by a monoclonal antibody (11F9) that binds to HsFpn with nanomolar affinity (Figure 1a–b), providing further support that HsFpn mediates Ca2+ transport. As the fragment of antigen-binding (Fab) of 11F9 is known to target the intracellular side of HsFpn (Figure 2a; Pan et al., 2020; Wilbon et al., 2023), we applied the Fab either to only the external side of the liposomes or to both sides of the liposomes, and found that the inhibition is significantly higher when Fab is present on both sides. This result indicates that HsFpn is incorporated into liposomes in both orientations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c–g). To understand the mechanism of Ca2+ transport by HsFpn, we first examined whether common ions, H+, Na+, K+, and Cl-, are involved or required for Ca2+ transport. We found that Ca2+ transport by HsFpn is not affected by a H+ gradient (Figure 1e–f and Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and that the absence of Na+, K+, or Cl- has no significant effect on Ca2+ transport (Figure 1—figure supplement 3). These results suggest that Fpn is a Ca2+ uniporter. If this is true, then Ca2+ transport should be electrogenic and sensitive to membrane potentials. We tested this in the following experiments. We measured Ca2+ transport at defined membrane potentials,+120 mV, 0 mV, and –120 mV, established by a K+ gradient in the presence of valinomycin, a K+ selective ionophore (Figure 1g). As shown in Figure 1g–h, Ca2+ transport is significantly enhanced at –120 mV and reduced at +120 mV, and Ca2+ transport at 0 mV is larger than that in the absence of a clamped membrane potential. These results are fully consistent with HsFpn being a Ca2+ uniporter. We then measured Ca2+ transport at different concentrations of Ca2+ ([Ca2+]), first in the absence of a preset membrane potential and then in the presence of –120 mV membrane potential (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a). We first monitored Ca2+ influx in the presence of a 100-fold K+ concentration gradient but in the absence of valinomycin. Under this condition, import of Ca2+ would build up a positive membrane potential that slows down further Ca2+ influx. After the influx reached a steady state (~460 s), we added valinomycin to clamp the membrane potential to –120 mV and we observed a large increase of Ca2+ influx. The rate of Ca2+ uptake in the second phase is faster than that in the first phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a). These results are consistent with HsFpn being a Ca2+ uniporter. The Michaelis-Menten constant, KM, for Ca2+ transport, calculated based on the initial rate of fluorescence increase in the second phase, is 48.5 (27.3–88.8) µM (95% confidence interval in parentheses) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4b). We also measured Ca2+ uptake in HEK cells expressing HsFpn and obtained a KM of 85.9 (36.6–193.0) µM (Figure 1—figure supplement 4c–d). ### Structure of HsFpn bound to Ca2+ We determined the structure of nanodisc-enclosed HsFpn-11F9 complex in the presence of 2 mM Ca2+ by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to an overall resolution of 3.0 Å (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Table 1). The density map reaches a resolution of ~2.4 Å in the transmembrane (TM) regions and allows for the building and refinement of a structural model that contains residues 15–240, 289–400, and 452–555, which covers all 12 TM helices (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). Residues 1–14, 241–288, 401–451, and 556–571, which are predicted to be disordered regions located to either the N- or C-terminus or loops between TM helices, are not resolved. The 12 TMs form two well-defined domains, with the N-terminal domain (NTD) composed of TM1–6 and the C-terminal domain (CTD) TM7–12 (Figure 2b). The current structure assumes an outward-facing conformation in which the NTD and CTD make contact on the intracellular side. The overall conformation of the Ca2+-bound HsFpn is similar to that of the Co2+-bound HsFpn (Wilbon et al., 2023; Figure 2e–g and Figure 2—figure supplement 3b). **Table 1.** Summary of cryo-EM data collection, processing, and refinement.

In the density map (Figure 2a), we noticed a non-protein density corralled by four helices (TM1, TM3, TM4, and TM6) in the NTD, and assigned it as a Ca2+ based on the following observations. This density was not present in previous structures of Co2+-bound HsFpn or a highly homologous Fpn from Tarsier monkey (Pan et al., 2020; Billesbølle et al., 2020; Wilbon et al., 2023). The side chains of five conserved residues, Asp39, Gln99, Asn100, Asn212, and Glu219, are within 4 Å of the presumed Ca2+ density (Figure 2b–c). The side chain positions of Gln99, Asn100, and Asn212 are defined by the density map, while these of Asp39 and Glu219 are deduced based on their backbone and partially resolved side chain densities. While in structures of Co2+-bound HsFpn (Wilbon et al., 2023; Billesbølle et al., 2020), the side chains of Asp39 and His43 point towards the central cavity between the NTD and CTD to form S1, the side chain of Asp39 in the current structure points towards the interior of the four-helical bundle to coordinate Ca2+ (Figure 2d). His43 also assumes a different rotamer conformation in the current structure (Figure 2d). When the NTD and CTD are aligned individually with their counterparts in the Co2+-bound HsFpn (Wilbon et al., 2023), the NTD has a root mean squared distance (RMSD) of 1.32 Å and the CTD 0.51 Å. The larger RMSD in the NTD is due to deviations of the extracellular halves of the TM helices and the extracellular loop between TM3–4 (Figure 2e–g). The bound Ca2+ is not solvent-accessible in the current structure. ### Validation of the Ca2+ binding site We validated the Ca2+ binding site by mutational studies. Both a single alanine mutation (Asp39Ala) and a triple alanine mutation (Gln99_Asn100_Glu219 to Ala) to the Ca2+ binding site show significantly reduced Ca2+ transport activity in the proteoliposome assay (Figure 3a–b). In contrast, the double alanine mutation to S2 (Cys326Ala_His507Ala) does not affect Ca2+ transport significantly (Figure 3a–b). We also measured Ca2+ uptake by HsFpn mutants expressed in HEK cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and found that single alanine mutations to residues at the Ca2+ binding site significantly impair Ca2+ transport activity, while mutation to His43 (at S1), which is one helical turn away from Asp39 at Ca2+ binding site, maintains high Ca2+ transport activity (Figure 3c–d). ![Figure 3.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/82947/elife-82947-fig3-v2.jpg) **Figure 3.:** (a) Ca2+ influx by WT (green), D39A (blue), and the triple mutant (Q99A_N100A_E219A, purple) of the Ca2+ binding site in proteoliposomes. We estimated Ca2+ binding affinity by isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). We found that Ca2+ binding is an endothermic process with a dissociation constant (KD) of ~32 µM (Figure 3e). Similar endothermic binding of Ca2+ was also reported in mouse Fpn and a bacterial homolog of Fpn (Deshpande et al., 2018). The 11F9 Fab does not interfere with or enhance Ca2+ binding as the HsFpn-11F9 complex has a similar Ca2+ binding affinity (KD = 20 ± 6 µM; ) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a). We then measured Ca2+ binding to HsFpn mutants, and found that single point mutations to residues at the Ca2+ binding site abolish Ca2+ binding (Figure 3f and Figure 3—figure supplement 2e–h). As a control, we measured Ca2+ binding to the His43Ala mutant and to the S2 mutant, and found that both mutants retain Ca2+ binding with affinities similar to that of the wild-type (WT; Figure 3g and Figure 3—figure supplement 2c). In addition, a Ca2+ binding site mutant, Gln99Ala, does not significantly change Co2+ binding affinity (KD = 226 ± 23 µM; Figure 3—figure supplement 2d). Asn212Ala does not significantly change Zn2+ binding to HsFpn (KD = 224 ± 30 µM) either (Figure 3—figure supplement 2i–j). Combined, these results provide further validation to the observed Ca2+ binding site in HsFpn. ### Competition between Ca2+ and Co2+ in HsFpn Next, we measured binding of Ca2+ in the presence of Co2+, and vice versa. In the presence of 2 mM Co2+, Ca2+ binding affinity is reduced by ~fourfold as shown in Figure 4a. The reduced binding is apparent both from the reduced heat absorption during the titration, and the reduced KD from fitting of the ITC data. We interpret the reduced Ca2+ binding in the presence of Co2+ as the loss of Asp39 to the coordination of Co2+ at S1 (Figure 2d). On the other hand, Co2+ binding affinity (KD) is not affected in the presence of 2 mM Ca2+, as shown in Figure 4b, although the amount of heat release is appreciably less in the presence of Ca2+. This result is similar to the effect of the S1 mutation on Co2+ binding (Asp39_His43 to Ala, KD = 266 ± 24 µM) (Pan et al., 2020). We then measured Ca2+ transport in the presence of Fe2+ or Co2+, and Fe2+ or Co2+ transport in the presence of Ca2+. We found that Fe2+ or Co2+ transport is not affected significantly in the presence of either 1.25 mM or 0.5 mM Ca2+ (Figure 4c–d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–f), but Ca2+ transport is significantly reduced in the presence of Fe2+ or Co2+ (Figure 4e–g and Figure 4—figure supplement 2c–e). These results are consistent with the structures and our understanding of Fe2+ and Ca2+ transport in Fpn. Fe2+ or Co2+ transport is mediated by both S1 and S2, and binding of Ca2+, which renders Asp39 unavailable, does not significantly affect Fe2+ or Co2+ transport because part of S1, His43, and the entire of S2 remain available to Fe2+ or Co2+ transport. On the other hand, Ca2+ transport is mediated by a single site and in the presence of Fe2+ or Co2+, Ca2+ binding site is impaired due to the loss of Asp39 and hence significantly reduced Ca2+ binding and transport (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a–c). Indeed, Asp39Ala single mutation significantly reduces Ca2+ transport (Figure 3a) but has a modest effect on Co2+ transport (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–b). Further studies are needed to dissect the intertwined transport pathways of Fe2+ and Ca2+ transport in Fpn. ## Discussion In summary, we show that HsFpn has a well-defined single Ca2+ binding site, and that HsFpn transports Ca2+. We also show that Ca2+ transport by HsFpn is not coupled to another ion and is diminished in the presence of Fe2+, however, Fe2+ transport is not sensitive to the presence of Ca2+. Our report of Ca2+ transport by HsFpn contradicts the conclusion from a previous study (Deshpande et al., 2018); however, the two studies also have common grounds. Deshpande et al. identified a Ca2+ binding site in the structure of BbFpn (Bdellovibrio bacteriovorus), a bacterial homolog of human Fpn (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a), and demonstrated Ca2+ binding to mouse Fpn, which is in agreement with our demonstration of a Ca2+ binding site in HsFpn. Deshpande et al. conclude that Ca2+ may serve as a bound “cofactor” required for Fe2+ transport (Deshpande et al., 2018), and our results imply that Fpn could transport Fe2+ while bound to a Ca2+. With the structure of Ca2+-bound HsFpn, we noticed that residues forming the Ca2+ binding site are conserved between BbFpn and HsFpn, except for Asn100 in HsFpn, which is Phe85 in BbFpn. The persistence of a Ca2+ binding site from bacteria to mammals suggests a conserved functional role of Ca2+, and future studies aimed at understanding the biological relevance of Ca2+ transport through Fpn will lead to understanding of regulations in iron homeostasis. Ca2+ binding and transport in HsFpn imposes constraint to the conceptualization of the Fe2+/2H+ antiport mechanism in the context of S1 and S2 of Fe2+ binding sites. In the absence of a bound Ca2+, export of one Fe2+ could be mediated through sequential occupation of S1 and S2 and structural changes that expose the binding sites to the extracellular side; and import of two H+ could be mediated by protonation of His43 at S1 and His507 at S2 followed by a structural change that exposes the two residues to the intracellular side. When Ca2+ is bound, Asp39 is not available to mediate Fe2+ export so that transport would likely be mediated by S2 only or by coalescing of His43 and S2 around a single Fe2+. Since we do not observe significant changes in Fe2+ transport in the presence and absence of Ca2+, it is likely that S1, or residue Asp39, has a more modest effect on Fe2+ transport, while S2 has a more prominent role. Results from our initial mutational studies on S1 and S2 are consistent with this hypothesis. Further studies are required to establish a mechanism of transport. Our discovery of Ca2+ transport in Fpn demonstrates a novel Ca2+ entry pathway in cells expressing Fpn, and our study establishes Fpn as a transporter capable of operating with two different transport mechanisms. Although we are not able to estimate the amount of Ca2+ uptake through HsFpn under physiological conditions to provide an interpretation for its cellular function, we speculate that Ca2+ entry through HsFpn is an important component contributing to iron homeostasis. ## Materials and methods **Key resources table**

Purification of HsFpn follows the same protocol reported for Tarsius syrichta Fpn (TsFpn) (Pan et al., 2020). Purified HsFpn was collected from size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) in the FPLC buffer containing 20 mM 4-(2-Hydroxyethyl)piperazine-1-ethanesulfonic acid (HEPES, pH7.5), 150 mM NaCl, and 1 mM (w/v) n-dodecyl-β-D-maltoside (DDM, Anatrace). Mutants were expressed and purified following the same protocol for the WT. ### Preparation of HsFpn-11F9 complex in nanodisc Membrane scaffold protein (MSP) 1D1 was expressed and purified following an established protocol (Martens et al., 2016). For nanodisc reconstitution, HsFpn, MSP1D1 and lipid mixture were mixed at a molar ratio of 1:2.5:50 and incubated on ice for 1 hr. Detergents were removed by the sequential addition of 60 mg/mL Biobeads SM2 (Bio-Rad) for three times over a 3-hr period. The sample was then incubated with Biobeads overnight at 4 °C. After removal of Biobeads, 11F9 was added to the sample at a molar ratio of 1.1:1 to HsFpn. The complex was incubated on ice for 30 min before being loaded onto a SEC column equilibrated with the FPLC buffer without detergent. The purified nanodisc sample was concentrated to 10 mg/ml and incubated with 2 mM CaCl2 for 30 min on ice before cryo-EM grid preparation. ### Cryo-EM sample preparation and data collection The cryo-EM grids were prepared using Thermo Fisher Vitrobot Mark IV. The Quantifoil R1.2/1.3 Cu grids were glow-discharged with air for 15 s at 10 mA using Plasma Cleaner (PELCO EasiGlow). Aliquots of 3.5 µl nanodisc sample were applied to the glow-discharged grids. After blotted with filter paper (Ted Pella, Inc) for 4.0 s, the grids were plunged into liquid ethane cooled with liquid nitrogen. A total of 4498 micrograph stacks were collected on a Titan Krios at 300 kV equipped with a K3 direct electron detector (Gatan) and a Quantum energy filter (Gatan) at a nominal magnification of 81,000×and defocus values from –2.5 µm to –0.8 µm. Each stack was exposed in the super-resolution mode with an exposing time of 0.0875 s per frame for a total of 40 frames per stack. The total dose was about 50 e-/Å2 for each stack. The stacks were motion corrected with MotionCor2 (Zheng et al., 2017) and binned 2-fold, resulting in a pixel size of 1.10 Å/pixel. In the meantime, dose weighting was performed (Grant and Grigorieff, 2015). The defocus values were estimated with Gctf (Zhang, 2016). ### Cryo-EM data processing A total of 2,184,301 particles were automatically picked based on a reference map of TsFpn-11F9 (EMD-21460) low-pass filtered to 20 Å in RELION 3.1 (Scheres, 2015, Scheres, 2012; Kimanius et al., 2016; Zivanov et al., 2018). Particles were extracted and imported to CryoSparc (Punjani et al., 2017) for 2D classification. A total of 1,329,782 particles were selected from good classes in 2D classification, which display recognizable structural features. Four 3D references were generated by ab initio reconstruction with limited particles from the best 2D classes. Multiple rounds of heterogeneous refinement were performed with particles selected from the 2D classification and four initial reference models until no more than 5% of input particles were classified into bad classes. A final of 437,959 particles after heterogeneous refinement were subjected to non-uniform (NU) refinement with an adaptive solvent mask. After handedness correction, local refinement and CTF refinement were performed with a soft mask around the Fpn and the Fv region of the Fab. Resolutions were estimated with the gold-standard Fourier shell correlation 0.143 criterion (Rosenthal and Henderson, 2003). Local resolution of the maps was estimated in CryoSparc (Punjani et al., 2017). ### Model building and refinement The structure of apo HsFpn (from PDB ID 6W4S) and 11F9 Fab (from PDB ID 6VYH) were individually docked into density maps in Chimera (Pettersen et al., 2004). All structure figures were prepared in Pymol and ChimeraX (Pettersen et al., 2021). ### Isothermal titration calorimetry The WT and mutant HsFpn proteins were purified as described above and concentrated to 50–75 μM (3–4.5 mg/mL) in the FPLC buffer. Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Mechanism of Ca2+ transport by ferroportin" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, including David Drew as the Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #1, and the evaluation has been overseen by Kenton Swartz as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Aashish Manglik (Reviewer #3).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Major concerns:

You have been able to robustly demonstrate Ca2+ binding. What is unclear is if Ca2+ is actually transported to a significant level? Is the Fpn protein just capable of one turnover in proteoliposomes? We highly recommend kinetics using 45CaCl2 (eg. PNAS E5354-E5362) to calculate actual Ca2+ turnover (kcat).

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors have been able to robustly demonstrate Ca2+ binding. What is unclear to me is how much Ca2+ is actually transported? Is the Fpn protein just capable of one turnover in proteoliposomes? The "cleanest" experiment would be to measure Ca2+ uptake using 45CaCl2 (eg. PNAS E5354-E5362) so one can calculate Vmax and kcat. From my understanding, metalloproteins do not necessarily use the optimum metal for catalysis, but the metal available in the appropriate concentration in where they function. I wonder if the Ca2+ site is just not selected against, because its not needed too, i.e., Ca2+ doesn't compete for Fe2+ uptake and the actual "turnover" for Ca2+ is very low?

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

The data reported here appear to be of high quality and are convincing; the experimental design is excellent and the necessary controls are appropriately employed. A couple of issues need clarification in the text. FPN is clearly an iron efflux pump and these studies make clear that Fpn can also import Ca2+, although it does not appear to function as an Fe2+-Ca2+ antiporter. What is less clear is whether Fpn will transport calcium bi-directionally. There are technical issues that would make this a bit hard to study, but if the authors think the answer is clear from their data, they should be explicit in explaining this. A further question that needs explaining is why bind and transport calcium? Cells have a high capacity for calcium flux independent of Fpn. Is there a physiological importance to this activity?

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claims.claim: S1 is composed of Asp39 and His43.
claims.source: Curiously, each ion binding site is composed of only two residues, Asp39 and His43 for S1, and Cys326 and His507 for S2, and it remains unsettled how S1 and S2 mediate coupled transport of Fe2+ and H+.
claims.evidence: This is supported by previous structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: S2 is composed of Cys326 and His507.
claims.source: Curiously, each ion binding site is composed of only two residues, Asp39 and His43 for S1, and Cys326 and His507 for S2, and it remains unsettled how S1 and S2 mediate coupled transport of Fe2+ and H+.
claims.evidence: This is supported by previous structural studies cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Asp39 is part of a Ca2+ binding site.
claims.source: In the current study, we found that Asp39 is also part of a Ca2+ binding site, and that mutation Asp39Ala almost completely eliminates Ca2+ transport but has a modest impact on Fe2+ transport, suggesting that S1 and S2 may have different roles in Fe2+ or H+ transport.
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural data in Figure 2 and functional data in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Mutation Asp39Ala almost completely eliminates Ca2+ transport but has a modest impact on Fe2+ transport.
claims.source: In the current study, we found that Asp39 is also part of a Ca2+ binding site, and that mutation Asp39Ala almost completely eliminates Ca2+ transport but has a modest impact on Fe2+ transport, suggesting that S1 and S2 may have different roles in Fe2+ or H+ transport.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3a-b and Figure 3—figure supplement 3a-b.

claims.claim: S1 and S2 may have different roles in Fe2+ or H+ transport.
claims.source: In the current study, we found that Asp39 is also part of a Ca2+ binding site, and that mutation Asp39Ala almost completely eliminates Ca2+ transport but has a modest impact on Fe2+ transport, suggesting that S1 and S2 may have different roles in Fe2+ or H+ transport.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of Asp39Ala mutation on Ca2+ versus Fe2+ transport.

claims.claim: Ca2+ is known to bind to mammalian Fpn.
claims.source: Ca2+ is known to bind to mammalian Fpn (Deshpande et al., 2018), but Ca2+ transport by Fpn has not been demonstrated and the role of Ca2+ in Fe2+ transport remains ambiguous.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Using Fpn expressed in Xenopus oocytes, Deshpande et al. found that Fe2+ export requires Ca2+, but Ca2+ is not transported by Fpn.
claims.source: Using Fpn expressed in Xenopus oocytes, Deshpande et al. found that Fe2+ export requires Ca2+, but Ca2+ is not transported by Fpn (Deshpande et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Several studies using purified Fpn reconstituted into liposomes found that Fe2+ transport occurs in the absence of Ca2+.
claims.source: More recently, several studies using purified Fpn reconstituted into liposomes found that Fe2+ transport occurs in the absence of Ca2+ (Li et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2020; Billesbølle et al., 2020), and that Ca2+ could potentiate Fe2+ transport under certain conditions (Li et al., 2020; Billesbølle et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Ca2+ could potentiate Fe2+ transport under certain conditions.
claims.source: More recently, several studies using purified Fpn reconstituted into liposomes found that Fe2+ transport occurs in the absence of Ca2+ (Li et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2020; Billesbølle et al., 2020), and that Ca2+ could potentiate Fe2+ transport under certain conditions (Li et al., 2020; Billesbølle et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Significant Ca2+ uptake was observed in proteoliposomes reconstituted with HsFpn.
claims.source: Significant Ca2+ uptake was observed in proteoliposomes reconstituted with HsFpn, as indicated by increased fluorescence of Fluo-4 trapped inside of the vesicles (Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claims.claim: Control liposomes that do not have HsFpn show minimal change in fluorescence.
claims.source: In contrast, control liposomes that do not have HsFpn show minimal change in fluorescence (Figure 1a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claims.claim: Ca2+ transport is inhibited by hepcidin.
claims.source: We also found that Ca2+ transport is inhibited by hepcidin and by a monoclonal antibody (11F9) that binds to HsFpn with nanomolar affinity (Figure 1a–b), providing further support that HsFpn mediates Ca2+ transport.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a-b.

claims.claim: Ca2+ transport is inhibited by a monoclonal antibody (11F9) that binds to HsFpn with nanomolar affinity.
claims.source: We also found that Ca2+ transport is inhibited by hepcidin and by a monoclonal antibody (11F9) that binds to HsFpn with nanomolar affinity (Figure 1a–b), providing further support that HsFpn mediates Ca2+ transport.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a-b and previous characterization of 11F9.

claims.claim: The Fab of 11F9 targets the intracellular side of HsFpn.
claims.source: As the fragment of antigen-binding (Fab) of 11F9 is known to target the intracellular side of HsFpn (Figure 2a; Pan et al., 2020; Wilbon et al., 2023), we applied the Fab either to only the external side of the liposomes or to both sides of the liposomes, and found that the inhibition is significantly higher when Fab is present on both sides.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and structural data in Figure 2a.

claims.claim: HsFpn is incorporated into liposomes in both orientations.
claims.source: This result indicates that HsFpn is incorporated into liposomes in both orientations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c–g).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential inhibition by Fab applied to different sides of liposomes, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c-g.

claims.claim: HsFpn expressed in HEK cells mediates Ca2+ uptake.
claims.source: We also examined HsFpn expressed in human embryonic kidney (HEK) cells and found that HsFpn mediates Ca2+ uptake (Figure 1c–d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c-d.

claims.claim: Ca2+ transport by HsFpn is not affected by a H+ gradient.
claims.source: We found that Ca2+ transport by HsFpn is not affected by a H+ gradient (Figure 1e–f and Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and that the absence of Na+, K+, or Cl- has no significant effect on Ca2+ transport (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e-f and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The absence of Na+, K+, or Cl- has no significant effect on Ca2+ transport.
claims.source: We found that Ca2+ transport by HsFpn is not affected by a H+ gradient (Figure 1e–f and Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and that the absence of Na+, K+, or Cl- has no significant effect on Ca2+ transport (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Fpn is a Ca2+ uniporter.
claims.source: These results suggest that Fpn is a Ca2+ uniporter.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of coupling to other ions and supported by membrane potential experiments.

claims.claim: Ca2+ transport is significantly enhanced at –120 mV and reduced at +120 mV.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 1g–h, Ca2+ transport is significantly enhanced at –120 mV and reduced at +120 mV, and Ca2+ transport at 0 mV is larger than that in the absence of a clamped membrane potential.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1g-h.

claims.claim: Ca2+ transport at 0 mV is larger than that in the absence of a clamped membrane potential.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 1g–h, Ca2+ transport is significantly enhanced at –120 mV and reduced at +120 mV, and Ca2+ transport at 0 mV is larger than that in the absence of a clamped membrane potential.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1g-h.

claims.claim: The Michaelis-Menten constant (KM) for Ca2+ transport in proteoliposomes is 48.5 (27.3–88.8) µM.
claims.source: The Michaelis-Menten constant, KM, for Ca2+ transport, calculated based on the initial rate of fluorescence increase in the second phase, is 48.5 (27.3–88.8) µM (95% confidence interval in parentheses) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and curve fitting shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4b.

claims.claim: The KM for Ca2+ transport in HEK cells expressing HsFpn is 85.9 (36.6–193.0) µM.
claims.source: We also measured Ca2+ uptake in HEK cells expressing HsFpn and obtained a KM of 85.9 (36.6–193.0) µM (Figure 1—figure supplement 4c–d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and curve fitting shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4c-d.

claims.claim: The structure of nanodisc-enclosed HsFpn-11F9 complex in the presence of 2 mM Ca2+ was determined by cryo-EM to an overall resolution of 3.0 Å.
claims.source: We determined the structure of nanodisc-enclosed HsFpn-11F9 complex in the presence of 2 mM Ca2+ by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to an overall resolution of 3.0 Å (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Table 1.

claims.claim: The density map reaches a resolution of ~2.4 Å in the transmembrane (TM) regions.
claims.source: The density map reaches a resolution of ~2.4 Å in the transmembrane (TM) regions and allows for the building and refinement of a structural model that contains residues 15–240, 289–400, and 452–555, which covers all 12 TM helices (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data and local resolution analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e.

claims.claim: The structural model contains residues 15–240, 289–400, and 452–555, which covers all 12 TM helices.
claims.source: The density map reaches a resolution of ~2.4 Å in the transmembrane (TM) regions and allows for the building and refinement of a structural model that contains residues 15–240, 289–400, and 452–555, which covers all 12 TM helices (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural model and density maps shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Residues 1–14, 241–288, 401–451, and 556–571 are not resolved.
claims.source: Residues 1–14, 241–288, 401–451, and 556–571, which are predicted to be disordered regions located to either the N- or C-terminus or loops between TM helices, are not resolved.
claims.evidence: This is based on the structural model and density maps.

claims.claim: The 12 TMs form two well-defined domains, with the N-terminal domain (NTD) composed of TM1–6 and the C-terminal domain (CTD) TM7–12.
claims.source: The 12 TMs form two well-defined domains, with the N-terminal domain (NTD) composed of TM1–6 and the C-terminal domain (CTD) TM7–12 (Figure 2b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2b.

claims.claim: The Ca2+-bound HsFpn assumes an outward-facing conformation in which the NTD and CTD make contact on the intracellular side.
claims.source: The current structure assumes an outward-facing conformation in which the NTD and CTD make contact on the intracellular side.
claims.evidence: This is based on the structural data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The overall conformation of the Ca2+-bound HsFpn is similar to that of the Co2+-bound HsFpn.
claims.source: The overall conformation of the Ca2+-bound HsFpn is similar to that of the Co2+-bound HsFpn (Wilbon et al., 2023; Figure 2e–g and Figure 2—figure supplement 3b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2e-g and Figure 2—figure supplement 3b.

claims.claim: A non-protein density corralled by four helices (TM1, TM3, TM4, and TM6) in the NTD was assigned as a Ca2+.
claims.source: In the density map (Figure 2a), we noticed a non-protein density corralled by four helices (TM1, TM3, TM4, and TM6) in the NTD, and assigned it as a Ca2+ based on the following observations.
claims.evidence: This is based on cryo-EM density map analysis shown in Figure 2a and 2c.

claims.claim: This density was not present in previous structures of Co2+-bound HsFpn or a highly homologous Fpn from Tarsier monkey.
claims.source: This density was not present in previous structures of Co2+-bound HsFpn or a highly homologous Fpn from Tarsier monkey (Pan et al., 2020; Billesbølle et al., 2020; Wilbon et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with previous structures cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Five conserved residues, Asp39, Gln99, Asn100, Asn212, and Glu219, are within 4 Å of the presumed Ca2+ density.
claims.source: The side chains of five conserved residues, Asp39, Gln99, Asn100, Asn212, and Glu219, are within 4 Å of the presumed Ca2+ density (Figure 2b–c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2b-c.

claims.claim: The side chain positions of Gln99, Asn100, and Asn212 are defined by the density map.
claims.source: The side chain positions of Gln99, Asn100, and Asn212 are defined by the density map, while these of Asp39 and Glu219 are deduced based on their backbone and partially resolved side chain densities.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM density map.

claims.claim: The side chains of Asp39 and Glu219 are deduced based on their backbone and partially resolved side chain densities.
claims.source: The side chain positions of Gln99, Asn100, and Asn212 are defined by the density map, while these of Asp39 and Glu219 are deduced based on their backbone and partially resolved side chain densities.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM density map.

claims.claim: In the Ca2+-bound structure, the side chain of Asp39 points towards the interior of the four-helical bundle to coordinate Ca2+.
claims.source: While in structures of Co2+-bound HsFpn (Wilbon et al., 2023; Billesbølle et al., 2020), the side chains of Asp39 and His43 point towards the central cavity between the NTD and CTD to form S1, the side chain of Asp39 in the current structure points towards the interior of the four-helical bundle to coordinate Ca2+ (Figure 2d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2d.

claims.claim: His43 assumes a different rotamer conformation in the Ca2+-bound structure compared to the Co2+-bound structure.
claims.source: His43 also assumes a different rotamer conformation in the current structure (Figure 2d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2d.

claims.claim: When the NTD and CTD are aligned individually with their counterparts in the Co2+-bound HsFpn, the NTD has a root mean squared distance (RMSD) of 1.32 Å and the CTD 0.51 Å.
claims.source: When the NTD and CTD are aligned individually with their counterparts in the Co2+-bound HsFpn (Wilbon et al., 2023), the NTD has a root mean squared distance (RMSD) of 1.32 Å and the CTD 0.51 Å.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural alignment calculations.

claims.claim: The larger RMSD in the NTD is due to deviations of the extracellular halves of the TM helices and the extracellular loop between TM3–4.
claims.source: The larger RMSD in the NTD is due to deviations of the extracellular halves of the TM helices and the extracellular loop between TM3–4 (Figure 2e–g).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 2e-g.

claims.claim: The bound Ca2+ is not solvent-accessible in the current structure.
claims.source: The bound Ca2+ is not solvent-accessible in the current structure.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the structure shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Single alanine mutation (Asp39Ala) to the Ca2+ binding site shows significantly reduced Ca2+ transport activity in the proteoliposome assay.
claims.source: Both a single alanine mutation (Asp39Ala) and a triple alanine mutation (Gln99_Asn100_Glu219 to Ala) to the Ca2+ binding site show significantly reduced Ca2+ transport activity in the proteoliposome assay (Figure 3a–b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a-b.

claims.claim: Triple alanine mutation (Gln99_Asn100_Glu219 to Ala) to the Ca2+ binding site shows significantly reduced Ca2+ transport activity in the proteoliposome assay.
claims.source: Both a single alanine mutation (Asp39Ala) and a triple alanine mutation (Gln99_Asn100_Glu219 to Ala) to the Ca2+ binding site show significantly reduced Ca2+ transport activity in the proteoliposome assay (Figure 3a–b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a-b.

claims.claim: The double alanine mutation to S2 (Cys326Ala_His507Ala) does not affect Ca2+ transport significantly.
claims.source: In contrast, the double alanine mutation to S2 (Cys326Ala_His507Ala) does not affect Ca2+ transport significantly (Figure 3a–b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a-b.

claims.claim: Single alanine mutations to residues at the Ca2+ binding site significantly impair Ca2+ transport activity in HEK cells.
claims.source: We also measured Ca2+ uptake by HsFpn mutants expressed in HEK cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and found that single alanine mutations to residues at the Ca2+ binding site significantly impair Ca2+ transport activity, while mutation to His43 (at S1), which is one helical turn away from Asp39 at Ca2+ binding site, maintains high Ca2+ transport activity (Figure 3c–d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c-d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Mutation to His43 (at S1), which is one helical turn away from Asp39 at Ca2+ binding site, maintains high Ca2+ transport activity.
claims.source: We also measured Ca2+ uptake by HsFpn mutants expressed in HEK cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and found that single alanine mutations to residues at the Ca2+ binding site significantly impair Ca2+ transport activity, while mutation to His43 (at S1), which is one helical turn away from Asp39 at Ca2+ binding site, maintains high Ca2+ transport activity (Figure 3c–d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c-d.

claims.claim: Ca2+ binding to HsFpn is an endothermic process with a dissociation constant (KD) of ~32 µM.
claims.source: We found that Ca2+ binding is an endothermic process with a dissociation constant (KD) of ~32 µM (Figure 3e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3e.

claims.claim: Similar endothermic binding of Ca2+ was also reported in mouse Fpn and a bacterial homolog of Fpn.
claims.source: Similar endothermic binding of Ca2+ was also reported in mouse Fpn and a bacterial homolog of Fpn (Deshpande et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The 11F9 Fab does not interfere with or enhance Ca2+ binding as the HsFpn-11F9 complex has a similar Ca2+ binding affinity (KD = 20 ± 6 µM).
claims.source: The 11F9 Fab does not interfere with or enhance Ca2+ binding as the HsFpn-11F9 complex has a similar Ca2+ binding affinity (KD = 20 ± 6 µM; ) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a.

claims.claim: Single point mutations to residues at the Ca2+ binding site abolish Ca2+ binding.
claims.source: We then measured Ca2+ binding to HsFpn mutants, and found that single point mutations to residues at the Ca2+ binding site abolish Ca2+ binding (Figure 3f and Figure 3—figure supplement 2e–h).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3f and Figure 3—figure supplement 2e-h.

claims.claim: The His43Ala mutant retains Ca2+ binding with affinity similar to that of the wild-type.
claims.source: As a control, we measured Ca2+ binding to the His43Ala mutant and to the S2 mutant, and found that both mutants retain Ca2+ binding with affinities similar to that of the wild-type (WT; Figure 3g and Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3g.

claims.claim: The S2 mutant retains Ca2+ binding with affinity similar to that of the wild-type.
claims.source: As a control, we measured Ca2+ binding to the His43Ala mutant and to the S2 mutant, and found that both mutants retain Ca2+ binding with affinities similar to that of the wild-type (WT; Figure 3g and Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claims.claim: A Ca2+ binding site mutant, Gln99Ala, does not significantly change Co2+ binding affinity (KD = 226 ± 23 µM).
claims.source: In addition, a Ca2+ binding site mutant, Gln99Ala, does not significantly change Co2+ binding affinity (KD = 226 ± 23 µM; Figure 3—figure supplement 2d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2d.

claims.claim: Asn212Ala does not significantly change Zn2+ binding to HsFpn (KD = 224 ± 30 µM).
claims.source: Asn212Ala does not significantly change Zn2+ binding to HsFpn (KD = 224 ± 30 µM) either (Figure 3—figure supplement 2i–j).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2i-j.

claims.claim: In the presence of 2 mM Co2+, Ca2+ binding affinity is reduced by ~fourfold.
claims.source: In the presence of 2 mM Co2+, Ca2+ binding affinity is reduced by ~fourfold as shown in Figure 4a.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4a.

claims.claim: The reduced Ca2+ binding in the presence of Co2+ is interpreted as the loss of Asp39 to the coordination of Co2+ at S1.
claims.source: We interpret the reduced Ca2+ binding in the presence of Co2+ as the loss of Asp39 to the coordination of Co2+ at S1 (Figure 2d).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural data shown in Figure 2d.

claims.claim: Co2+ binding affinity (KD) is not affected in the presence of 2 mM Ca2+.
claims.source: On the other hand, Co2+ binding affinity (KD) is not affected in the presence of 2 mM Ca2+, as shown in Figure 4b, although the amount of heat release is appreciably less in the presence of Ca2+.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4b.

claims.claim: The amount of heat release during Co2+ binding is appreciably less in the presence of Ca2+.
claims.source: On the other hand, Co2+ binding affinity (KD) is not affected in the presence of 2 mM Ca2+, as shown in Figure 4b, although the amount of heat release is appreciably less in the presence of Ca2+.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 4b.

claims.claim: The preservation of Co2+ binding in the presence of Ca2+ is interpreted as the preservation of Co2+ binding at S2, which is not affected by Ca2+ binding.
claims.source: We interpret this result as the preservation of Co2+ binding at S2, which is not affected by Ca2+ binding.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the structural understanding of S1 and S2.

claims.claim: Fe2+ or Co2+ transport is not affected significantly in the presence of either 1.25 mM or 0.5 mM Ca2+.
claims.source: We found that Fe2+ or Co2+ transport is not affected significantly in the presence of either 1.25 mM or 0.5 mM Ca2+ (Figure 4c–d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–f), but Ca2+ transport is significantly reduced in the presence of Fe2+ or Co2+ (Figure 4e–g and Figure 4—figure supplement 2c–e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c-d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a-f.

claims.claim: Ca2+ transport is significantly reduced in the presence of Fe2+ or Co2+.
claims.source: We found that Fe2+ or Co2+ transport is not affected significantly in the presence of either 1.25 mM or 0.5 mM Ca2+ (Figure 4c–d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–f), but Ca2+ transport is significantly reduced in the presence of Fe2+ or Co2+ (Figure 4e–g and Figure 4—figure supplement 2c–e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e-g and Figure 4—figure supplement 2c-e.

claims.claim: Fe2+ or Co2+ transport is mediated by both S1 and S2.
claims.source: These results are consistent with the structures and our understanding of Fe2+ and Ca2+ transport in Fpn. Fe2+ or Co2+ transport is mediated by both S1 and S2, and binding of Ca2+, which renders Asp39 unavailable, does not significantly affect Fe2+ or Co2+ transport because part of S1, His43, and the entire of S2 remain available to Fe2+ or Co2+ transport.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural and functional data.

claims.claim: Binding of Ca2+, which renders Asp39 unavailable, does not significantly affect Fe2+ or Co2+ transport because part of S1, His43, and the entire of S2 remain available to Fe2+ or Co2+ transport.
claims.source: These results are consistent with the structures and our understanding of Fe2+ and Ca2+ transport in Fpn. Fe2+ or Co2+ transport is mediated by both S1 and S2, and binding of Ca2+, which renders Asp39 unavailable, does not significantly affect Fe2+ or Co2+ transport because part of S1, His43, and the entire of S2 remain available to Fe2+ or Co2+ transport.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural and functional data.

claims.claim: Ca2+ transport is mediated by a single site.
claims.source: On the other hand, Ca2+ transport is mediated by a single site and in the presence of Fe2+ or Co2+, Ca2+ binding site is impaired due to the loss of Asp39 and hence significantly reduced Ca2+ binding and transport (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a–c).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural and functional data.

claims.claim: In the presence of Fe2+ or Co2+, Ca2+ binding site is impaired due to the loss of Asp39 and hence significantly reduced Ca2+ binding and transport.
claims.source: On the other hand, Ca2+ transport is mediated by a single site and in the presence of Fe2+ or Co2+, Ca2+ binding site is impaired due to the loss of Asp39 and hence significantly reduced Ca2+ binding and transport (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a–c).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural and functional data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3a-c.

claims.claim: Asp39Ala single mutation significantly reduces Ca2+ transport but has a modest effect on Co2+ transport.
claims.source: Indeed, Asp39Ala single mutation significantly reduces Ca2+ transport (Figure 3a) but has a modest effect on Co2+ transport (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 3a-b.

claims.claim: HsFpn has a well-defined single Ca2+ binding site.
claims.source: In summary, we show that HsFpn has a well-defined single Ca2+ binding site, and that HsFpn transports Ca2+.
claims.evidence: This is supported by structural data in Figure 2 and binding data in Figure 3.

claims.claim: HsFpn transports Ca2+.
claims.source: In summary, we show that HsFpn has a well-defined single Ca2+ binding site, and that HsFpn transports Ca2+.
claims.evidence: This is supported by transport data in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Ca2+ transport by HsFpn is not coupled to another ion.
claims.source: We also show that Ca2+ transport by HsFpn is not coupled to another ion and is diminished in the presence of Fe2+, however, Fe2+ transport is not sensitive to the presence of Ca2+.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1e-h and Figure 1—figure supplement 2-3.

claims.claim: Ca2+ transport is diminished in the presence of Fe2+.
claims.source: We also show that Ca2+ transport by HsFpn is not coupled to another ion and is diminished in the presence of Fe2+, however, Fe2+ transport is not sensitive to the presence of Ca2+.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4e-g.

claims.claim: Fe2+ transport is not sensitive to the presence of Ca2+.
claims.source: We also show that Ca2+ transport by HsFpn is not coupled to another ion and is diminished in the presence of Fe2+, however, Fe2+ transport is not sensitive to the presence of Ca2+.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4c-d.

claims.claim: The report of Ca2+ transport by HsFpn contradicts the conclusion from a previous study by Deshpande et al.
claims.source: Our report of Ca2+ transport by HsFpn contradicts the conclusion from a previous study (Deshpande et al., 2018); however, the two studies also have common grounds.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature.

claims.claim: Deshpande et al. identified a Ca2+ binding site in the structure of BbFpn, a bacterial homolog of human Fpn.
claims.source: Deshpande et al. identified a Ca2+ binding site in the structure of BbFpn (Bdellovibrio bacteriovorus), a bacterial homolog of human Fpn (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a), and demonstrated Ca2+ binding to mouse Fpn, which is in agreement with our demonstration of a Ca2+ binding site in HsFpn.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Deshpande et al. demonstrated Ca2+ binding to mouse Fpn.
claims.source: Deshpande et al. identified a Ca2+ binding site in the structure of BbFpn (Bdellovibrio bacteriovorus), a bacterial homolog of human Fpn (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a), and demonstrated Ca2+ binding to mouse Fpn, which is in agreement with our demonstration of a Ca2+ binding site in HsFpn.

results.result: HsFpn mediates Ca2+ transport as demonstrated by Ca2+ uptake in proteoliposomes and HEK cells, which is inhibited by hepcidin and the 11F9 antibody.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C26-29, C32, and C83 collectively demonstrate Ca2+ transport by HsFpn through multiple experimental systems (proteoliposomes and HEK cells) with appropriate controls (empty liposomes/cells) and specific inhibitors (hepcidin, 11F9 antibody). The convergence of evidence from different experimental approaches strongly supports this major finding.

results.result: Ca2+ transport by HsFpn is not coupled to other ions (H+, Na+, K+, Cl-) and is electrogenic, functioning as a Ca2+ uniporter with voltage-dependent transport.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C33-37, and C84 demonstrate through systematic ion substitution experiments and membrane potential manipulations that Ca2+ transport is independent of other ions and voltage-dependent. The data showing enhanced transport at -120 mV and reduced transport at +120 mV (C36) is consistent with electrogenic uniport mechanism.

results.result: The cryo-EM structure of Ca2+-bound HsFpn at 3.0 Å resolution reveals a single Ca2+ binding site in the NTD formed by five conserved residues (Asp39, Gln99, Asn100, Asn212, Glu219), distinct from the Fe2+ binding sites S1 and S2.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C40-42, C44-45, C47, C49, and C82 are supported by high-resolution cryo-EM data with appropriate resolution (3.0 Å overall, ~2.4 Å in TM regions). The identification of the Ca2+ binding site is based on density map analysis, structural comparison with previous structures, and proximity of coordinating residues. The structural data quality metrics in Table 1 support the model.

results.result: Mutagenesis studies validate the Ca2+ binding site: mutations of Ca2+ binding site residues (Asp39Ala, Gln99Ala, Asn100Ala, Glu219Ala) abolish or significantly reduce Ca2+ transport and binding, while mutations to S2 (Cys326Ala_His507Ala) or His43Ala do not affect Ca2+ transport.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-20, C57-61, C65-67 provide comprehensive mutational validation using both transport assays (proteoliposomes and HEK cells) and binding assays (ITC). The differential effects of mutations at the Ca2+ binding site versus control sites (S2, His43) provide strong support for the structural assignment. The consistency across multiple experimental approaches strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Ca2+ binds to HsFpn with a KD of ~32 μM (or 20 ± 6 μM for HsFpn-11F9 complex) in an endothermic process as measured by ITC.
results.evaluation: Claims C62 and C64 are supported by ITC measurements shown in Figure 3e and Figure 3—figure supplement 2a. The similar binding affinities between HsFpn alone and the HsFpn-11F9 complex indicate that the Fab does not interfere with Ca2+ binding. The endothermic nature is consistent with previous reports (C63).

results.result: The KM for Ca2+ transport is 48.5 (27.3–88.8) μM in proteoliposomes and 85.9 (36.6–193.0) μM in HEK cells expressing HsFpn.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-39 are supported by dose-response experiments with Michaelis-Menten curve fitting shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4b-d. The similar KM values between the two systems (within the same order of magnitude) support the physiological relevance of the findings. The 95% confidence intervals are provided.

results.result: Ca2+ and Fe2+/Co2+ compete for binding and transport: Ca2+ transport is significantly inhibited by Fe2+/Co2+, but Fe2+/Co2+ transport is not affected by Ca2+. Ca2+ binding affinity is reduced ~4-fold in the presence of Co2+, while Co2+ binding affinity is preserved in the presence of Ca2+.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C70-76, C80, C85-86 demonstrate asymmetric competition through ITC binding studies and transport assays in both proteoliposomes and HEK cells. The interpretation (C71, C74, C80) that this reflects loss of Asp39 to Co2+ at S1 while S2 remains available is consistent with the structural data. The convergence of binding and transport data supports this mechanism.

results.result: Structural comparison reveals that in the Ca2+-bound structure, Asp39 reorients toward the Ca2+ binding site (away from S1), His43 adopts a different rotamer, and the NTD shows conformational changes (RMSD 1.32 Å) particularly in extracellular regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-55 are supported by structural comparisons between Ca2+-bound and Co2+-bound HsFpn shown in Figure 2d-g. The RMSD calculations and identification of specific conformational changes are based on structural alignment. These observations provide mechanistic insight into how Ca2+ and Fe2+ binding are mutually exclusive at Asp39.

results.result: HsFpn is incorporated into liposomes in both orientations, as demonstrated by differential inhibition when 11F9 Fab (which targets the intracellular side) is applied to one or both sides of the liposomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-31 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c-g showing greater inhibition when Fab is present on both sides versus only the outside. This inference is logical given the known binding site of 11F9 Fab and provides important context for interpreting the transport assays.

results.result: S1 (particularly Asp39) has a modest effect on Fe2+ transport while S2 has a more prominent role, whereas Ca2+ transport is mediated by a single site that includes Asp39.
results.evaluation: Claims C21, C77-79, C94-95 represent interpretations and inferences based on the differential effects of mutations and competition experiments. While the data (C20, C81) show that Asp39Ala has modest effects on Fe2+/Co2+ transport but major effects on Ca2+ transport, the mechanistic interpretation about the relative roles of S1 and S2 in Fe2+ transport requires additional direct evidence. The authors acknowledge this needs "further studies" in the Discussion.

results.result: Background claims about ferroportin: Fpn is the only known Fe2+ exporter in humans, encoded by SLC40A1, functions as a Fe2+/2H+ exchanger, is regulated by hepcidin, and has two metal binding sites (S1: Asp39/His43; S2: Cys326/His507).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-2, C7-14, C16-18 represent established knowledge supported by multiple citations to the literature and previous work by the authors. These provide necessary context for the current study and are well-documented in the field.

results.result: The current findings contradict Deshpande et al. (2018) regarding Ca2+ transport but agree on Ca2+ binding; previous studies showed Fe2+ transport occurs without Ca2+ but Ca2+ may potentiate Fe2+ transport.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-25, C87-90 accurately represent the literature and acknowledge the contradiction with Deshpande et al. regarding Ca2+ transport while noting areas of agreement (Ca2+ binding). This contextualization is appropriate and the authors provide a reasonable reconciliation of the findings.

results.result: The Ca2+ binding site is conserved between bacterial (BbFpn) and human Fpn (except Asn100/Phe85), suggesting a conserved functional role for Ca2+.
results.evaluation: Claim C92 is supported by structural comparison (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a), but claim C93 about conserved functional role is speculative. While evolutionary conservation often implies functional importance, this requires experimental validation in the bacterial homolog and other species. The authors appropriately frame this as speculation requiring "future studies."

results.result: The discovery establishes Fpn as a dual-function transporter (Fe2+/2H+ antiporter and Ca2+ uniporter) representing a novel Ca2+ entry pathway that may regulate iron homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-97 are supported by the demonstrated Ca2+ uniport and previously established Fe2+/2H+ antiport functions. However, claims C98-99 about physiological significance and regulation of iron homeostasis are speculative. The authors acknowledge they "are not able to estimate the amount of Ca2+ uptake through HsFpn under physiological conditions." The physiological relevance requires additional in vivo studies.

results.result: The electroneutral Fe2+/2H+ transport mechanism is likely an adaptation to overcome negative resting membrane potential.
results.evaluation: Claim C15 is a speculative interpretation about evolutionary adaptation. While the reasoning is logical (electroneutral transport would avoid working against membrane potential), this evolutionary interpretation lacks direct experimental support and represents speculation rather than demonstrated fact.

results.result: The Ca2+ density was not present in previous Co2+-bound structures; side chains of Gln99, Asn100, Asn212 are defined by density while Asp39 and Glu219 are deduced from backbone and partial side chain densities.
results.evaluation: Claims C48, C50-51 describe the structural analysis methodology and quality of the density map. The acknowledgment that some side chains (Asp39, Glu219) are deduced rather than fully resolved is appropriate transparency about model uncertainty. The overall assignment is supported by the convergence with functional data.

results.result: The bound Ca2+ is not solvent-accessible in the current outward-facing structure.
results.evaluation: Claim C56 is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2. This observation is important for understanding the transport mechanism, as it implies conformational changes are required for Ca2+ release, consistent with an alternating access mechanism.

results.result: Similar endothermic Ca2+ binding was reported in mouse Fpn and bacterial Fpn homolog.
results.evaluation: Claim C63 is supported by citation to Deshpande et al. (2018). This provides validation that the endothermic binding observed is consistent with previous findings and not an artifact of the current experimental system.

results.result: Ca2+ binding site mutations (Gln99Ala, Asn212Ala) do not significantly affect Co2+ or Zn2+ binding, demonstrating specificity of the Ca2+ binding site.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-69 are supported by ITC data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2d, i-j. These control experiments demonstrate that the Ca2+ binding site is distinct from transition metal binding sites and that mutations at the Ca2+ site do not globally disrupt protein structure or metal binding capacity.

results.result: Asp39Ala mutation significantly reduces Ca2+ transport but has only modest effect on Co2+ transport.
results.evaluation: Claim C81 is supported by experimental data in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 3a-b. This differential effect is key evidence supporting the interpretation that Asp39 is more critical for Ca2+ transport than for Fe2+/Co2+ transport, consistent with the structural model.

results.result: Fpn could transport Fe2+ while bound to Ca2+.
results.evaluation: Claim C91 is an implication based on the observation that Fe2+ transport is not significantly affected by Ca2+ presence (C86). However, this does not directly demonstrate simultaneous binding or transport. The claim requires additional experiments, such as structural determination of a ternary complex or direct measurement of Fe2+ transport in Ca2+-bound Fpn.
